title: Sum of Proper Divisors s(n)
content: The formalization defines $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d | n} d$ as the sum of all divisors via Mathlib's `Nat.divisors`, then $s(n) = \sigma(n) - n$ as the sum of proper divisors (the aliquot sum). An alternative definition `s_alt` sums over `Nat.properDivisors` directly, and an axiom asserts equivalence for $n > 0$. For example, $s(6) = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6$, making 6 a perfect number. The function $s$ is the central object in the EGPS conjecture.

title: Perfect, Deficient, and Abundant Numbers
content: Classifies natural numbers by the relationship of $s(n)$ to $n$: **perfect** if $s(n) = n$ (e.g., 6 = 1+2+3, 28 = 1+2+4+7+14), **deficient** if $s(n) < n$ (e.g., all primes), **abundant** if $s(n) > n$ (e.g., 12 with $s(12) = 16$). Perfect numbers have been studied since Euclid, who proved $2^{p-1}(2^p-1)$ is perfect when $2^p-1$ is prime. Whether odd perfect numbers exist remains one of the oldest open questions in mathematics.

title: Natural Density Framework
content: Natural density is defined via the counting function $|A \cap [1,x]|$ and the limit $|A \cap [1,x]|/x \to d$ as $x \to \infty$. A set has zero density if this ratio tends to 0—informally, its elements become vanishingly rare. Examples: the primes have density 0 (by the prime number theorem, $\pi(x)/x \to 0$), sums of two squares have density 0 ($\sim cx/\sqrt{\log x}$), even numbers have density $1/2$. The EGPS conjecture is fundamentally about preservation of zero density under the map $n \mapsto s(n)$.

title: The Preimage s⁻¹(A)
content: Defines the set-theoretic preimage $s^{-1}(A) = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : s(n) \in A\}$. The EGPS conjecture asks whether $d(A) = 0$ implies $d(s^{-1}(A)) = 0$. The fiber $s^{-1}(\{k\})$ for a single value $k$ can be empty (if $k$ is untouchable), finite, or infinite. The conjecture concerns the aggregate density of fibers over all $k \in A$.

title: The EGPS Conjecture (1990, OPEN)
content: The Erdős-Granville-Pomerance-Spiro conjecture: if $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ has density 0, then $s^{-1}(A) = \{n : s(n) \in A\}$ must also have density 0. Equivalently, "sparse" target sets cannot attract a positive fraction of all integers under the sum-of-proper-divisors map. This is Problem #955 in the Erdős Problems database and remains open in full generality despite substantial partial progress. It is a fundamental question about the regularity of divisor-sum fibers.

title: Asymmetry of s: Forward vs Backward
content: The function $s$ exhibits a striking asymmetry. In the **forward direction**, $s$ can amplify density: there exist zero-density sets $A$ whose image $s(A)$ has positive density (e.g., $A$ = semiprimes $pq$, where $s(pq) = 1 + p + q$ covers a positive-density set). In the **backward direction**, large sets can have empty preimages: untouchable numbers like 2 and 5 are never $s(n)$ for any $n$. The EGPS conjecture concerns only the backward direction: does small $A$ force small $s^{-1}(A)$? The untouchable phenomenon shows the converse (large $A$ $\Rightarrow$ large $s^{-1}(A)$) is false.
mathContext: $\exists A: d(A) = 0 \text{ but } d(s(A)) > 0$; $\exists A: d(A) > 0 \text{ but } s^{-1}(A) = \emptyset$

title: Partial Results: Pollack, Troupe
content:
Three key partial results verify the conjecture for specific structured sets.

**Pollack (2014)**: Proved EGPS for $A$ = primes, using deep results on the distribution of $s(n)$ modulo primes. Since $s(n) \equiv -(n + \sigma(n)) \pmod{p}$, the key is showing $s(n)$ is equidistributed modulo most primes.

**Troupe (2015)**: Extended to integers with unusually many prime factors ($\omega(n) > k \log\log n$ for some $k$).

**Troupe (2020)**: Proved for $A$ = sums of two squares, exploiting the Landau-Ramanujan density $\sim cx/\sqrt{\log x}$ and multiplicative structure. Each proof requires specialized analytic techniques.
mathContext: $d(\{p \text{ prime}\}) = 0 \Rightarrow d(s^{-1}(\text{primes})) = 0$; similarly for sums of two squares

title: The PPT Threshold: x^{1/2+o(1)}
content: **Pollack-Pomerance-Thompson (2018)** proved the conjecture for all sets $A$ with $|A \cap [1,x]| \leq x^{1/2+o(1)}$—any set sparser than $x^{1/2}$ satisfies EGPS. The exponent $1/2$ arises from the growth bound $s(n) \leq n \cdot (2 + \log\log n)$: since $s$ maps $[1,x]$ into $[1, O(x \log\log x)]$, sets growing slower than the square root of the range cannot accumulate enough preimages. The corollary `sparse_sets_work` is a direct application. Closing the gap between this threshold and general zero-density sets is the main open challenge.

title: Growth Bound on s(n)
content: The axiom $s(n) \leq n(2 + \log\log n)$ captures the average growth rate of the aliquot sum. This bound follows from the well-known estimate $\sigma(n)/n \leq 1 + \sum_{p | n} 1/(p-1) \leq 2 + \log\log n$ for most $n$. It explains why the PPT threshold is $1/2$: the image of $[1,x]$ under $s$ lands in $[1, O(x \log\log x)]$, and sets of size $\leq x^{1/2+o(1)}$ are too sparse relative to this range to capture a positive fraction of inputs.
